#2595. NFL's new safety rule brings suspensions, but Buccaneers are clear

The NFL's revised player safety policy has introduced a new consequence for repeat offenders, with certain violations now carrying the possibility of a one-game suspension. As players around the league begin accumulating strikes under the new system, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers remain absent from a recently published tracker identifying potential suspension candidates.

The NFL and NFL Players Association announced the changes on August 26, establishing a disciplinary system targeting five specific violations: hip-drop tackles, horse-collar tackles, launching, hits on defenseless players, and blindside blocks. Players who commit three violations of the same designated rule face a one-game suspension, making repeated dangerous techniques a potential personnel concern rather than simply a financial penalty.

The policy also changes how fines are handled. Players with only one qualifying violation can recover 50% of their fine at the end of the season, while certain isolated offenses are eligible for a full refund. Although every player entered the 2026 regular season with a clean slate, violations can carry into future seasons, extending the consequences beyond a single year.

The league has also placed greater responsibility on coaching staffs. Coaches must join meetings with players approaching the suspension threshold, while organizations that accumulate excessive safety violations can face additional financial penalties. The changes are intended to address repeated dangerous conduct without imposing the same consequences on players who commit isolated mistakes.

According to a November 12 report from Logan Ulrich of NFL Trade Rumors, players across the league have already accumulated violations that could count toward suspensions. The tracker identifies New York Jets safety Minkah Fitzpatrick and San Francisco 49ers linebacker Fred Warner among those under additional scrutiny, although the listed violations fall into different categories and do not necessarily put either player one infraction away from suspension.

For Tampa Bay, the notable development is that no Buccaneers players appear on the published tracker. That does not establish that every player has avoided a safety-related fine, but the report does not identify anyone on the roster as having accumulated a qualifying regular-season violation.

The distinction is important because Tampa Bay has already had a player penalized for an offense covered by the new policy. Buccaneers linebacker David Walker received a $6,254 fine for a blindside block during the first week of the preseason, according to NBC Sports. However, the three-strike system did not take effect until the regular season, meaning Walker's preseason fine does not count toward a potential suspension.

The revised policy adds another consideration for Todd Bowles' defense, which often uses pressure packages and defensive backs near the line of scrimmage. Those responsibilities demand quick reactions and physical play, but the new disciplinary system increases the importance of proper tackling technique and avoiding repeated violations.

A suspension could also create challenges beyond the individual player. Losing a starter for one game would force adjustments to the defensive rotation, potentially increasing the workload for reserves or requiring changes to personnel packages. That makes monitoring violations increasingly important as teams navigate injuries and prepare for late-season matchups.

For now, the Buccaneers have no players identified in NFL Trade Rumors' November 12 tracker, an encouraging distinction as the league begins enforcing its revised disciplinary approach. This absence is not an official clearance from the NFL, but it suggests Tampa Bay has no players publicly flagged by the report as accumulating strikes toward a suspension.

#2592. Andreeva beats Pegula to reach WTA Finals championship match

French Open champion Mirra Andreeva beat American Jessica Pegula 6-3, 6-4 on Saturday to reach the WTA Finals championship match in Indian Wells, California.

With the semi-final win the 19-year-old Russian -- who won her maiden major at Roland Garros this year -- is assured of rising from third to second in the world rankings.

On Sunday she will face either Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova or Ukraine's Elina Svitolina for the title in the elite season-ending event, which was moved from Saudi Arabia to California in July because of war in the Middle East.

Andreeva remained unbeaten in her WTA Finals singles debut, having posted round robin victories over sixth-ranked Svitolina, world number two Aryna Sabalenka and Diana Shnaider.

For Pegula it was a match of missed chances, the fifth-ranked American unable to build on early breaks in both sets.

Andreeva double-faulted on break point to give Pegula a 2-1 lead in the opening set.

But the Russian broke back immediately, whipping a crosscourt forehand winner on her third break chance to make it 2-2.

Andreeva saved a pair of break points in the fifth game and broke again for a 5-3 lead.

Pegula had a chance to extend the set in the next game, but on break point she smashed what looked to be an easy backhand at the net past the baseline and Andreeva held to pocket the first.

Andreeva double-faulted to give Pegula a break chance in the fourth game of the second and the American converted for an imposing 3-1 lead.

But once again Andreeva broke back immediately, and broke again for a 4-3 lead.

She closed out the win after one hour and 25 minutes, giving herself a match point with an overhead winner before Pegula sent a backhand long.

#2590. Phoenix might be figuring things out, one stop at a time

Need a little hope? Looking for something to give you those warm and fuzzies as you sip your morning coffee? The sugar and cream aren't doing enough to brighten your day? Well, for all the ugly statistics we've been compiling about the Phoenix Suns lately, here's one that might make that coffee taste a little sweeter.

Through the first six games of the regular season, Phoenix ranked dead last in the NBA in defensive rating, surrendering a staggering 124.5 points per 100 possessions. It was an atrocious start, one that had us questioning whether this team possessed the personnel, discipline, or defensive identity necessary to compete night in and night out.

But since then? Things have changed considerably. Over their last five games, the Suns have posted a defensive rating of 109.0, the sixth-best mark in the NBA during that stretch. Their net rating has climbed to +4.2, ranking ninth in the league, a significant improvement from the -10.3 net rating that placed them 25th during their first six games.

That's a pretty substantial turnaround in a relatively short period of time.

And perhaps the most encouraging part is that those numbers include the absolute shellacking Phoenix suffered at the hands of the Spurs. Even with that disaster factored into the equation, the Suns have managed to establish themselves as one of the league's more effective defensive teams over their last five outings.

Now, does that mean all their problems have magically disappeared? Of course not. The rebounding remains atrocious, the lack of size continues to create significant disadvantages, and the questions surrounding roster construction and player fit aren't going anywhere anytime soon. But there is something encouraging about watching this team begin to stabilize defensively.

Much like last season, Phoenix stumbled out of the gate, struggling to establish any semblance of consistency before gradually finding its footing. And while we're still dealing with a relatively small sample size, the defensive improvement suggests that some of the early growing pains are beginning to subside.

The rotations are becoming more connected. The effort is more consistent. And the Suns are beginning to demonstrate they can make life difficult for opposing offenses, despite the physical limitations that continue to plague this roster.

There's still plenty of work to be done, and nobody should be throwing a parade over five games of improved defensive efficiency. But considering where this team stood after six games, seeing Phoenix climb from the league's worst defensive rating to the sixth-best over its next five is certainly worth acknowledging.

The defense is giving us something to feel good about. Perhaps it's a reminder that sometimes these things take time. I'll be the first to admit that I'm guilty of overreacting. I constantly find myself mining statistics, searching for numbers that either validate what I'm witnessing while watching these basketball games or challenge the conclusions I've already started forming. That's always the fascinating part of analyzing sports. There's the eye test, there's the data test, and somewhere in between lies the reality of what's actually happening on the court. And sometimes, multiple things can be true simultaneously.

The Phoenix Suns can be atrocious on the boards while still developing into a good defensive team. Those two realities aren't mutually exclusive, and we're beginning to see evidence of that as Phoenix demonstrates an improved ability to shut down opposing offenses for extended stretches, creating enough separation to secure victories.

The issues with rim deterrence remain, and opposing teams continue to exploit the Suns' lack of size around the basket. But on the perimeter? Things are beginning to look considerably better. Through the first six games of the season, Phoenix was allowing opponents to shoot 40.3% from beyond the arc, the second-worst mark in the NBA. It was a troubling statistic that reflected a defense struggling with rotations, communication, and the ability to consistently contest shots. Since then, that number has dropped to 33.9%, the 10th-best mark in the league during a five-game stretch in which the Suns have gone 4-1.

Part of it can certainly be attributed to regression toward the mean. Opponents were unlikely to continue shooting above 40% from deep indefinitely. But dismissing the entire improvement as statistical normalization would overlook the tangible progress we're witnessing from Phoenix defensively. The individual numbers help illustrate that improvement.

During the first six games, opponents were shooting 46.7% from three against Dillon Brooks. Over the last five, that number has dropped to 37.7%. Still not particularly impressive, but considerably better than what we witnessed during the opening stretch. Miles Bridges, who appeared lost on more than a few defensive rotations early in the season, has experienced a similar improvement. Opponents were shooting 38.1% from beyond the arc against him during the first six games. That number has since fallen to 34.7%.

These aren't insignificant developments. They're signs of players beginning to understand their responsibilities, recognize rotations, and operate with greater cohesion within Jordan Ott's defensive system.

There's another factor contributing to the increased defensive intensity. The bench. Jordan Goodwin has been fantastic over the last two games, bringing the kind of relentless energy and defensive aggression that can completely alter the complexion of a basketball game. Ryan Dunn has also begun making a more noticeable impact, using his length, athleticism, and defensive instincts to disrupt opposing offenses. Together, they've helped give Phoenix something that was desperately missing during the early portion of the season: a second unit capable of changing the momentum of a game through defensive effort.

The numbers reflect that impact. Through the first six games, the Suns' bench posted a net rating of +1.5. Over the last five games, that number has improved to +5.3. That's meaningful progress, particularly for a team whose starting lineup continues to struggle with consistency and finding the right combinations.

The bench has become a catalyst for much of the Suns' recent success, providing the defensive intensity, cohesion, and energy that have helped stabilize a team that looked completely disjointed at the start of the season.

Does five games of improved defensive performance mean Phoenix has solved all its problems? Certainly not. The rebounding remains a disaster, the interior defense still needs significant attention, and the roster continues to present challenges that aren't going to disappear overnight. But perhaps that's the lesson here. As much as we want immediate answers, as much as we want the statistics to confirm our suspicions after every game, sometimes a team needs time to figure out how its pieces fit together. While the Suns are still a work in progress, the defensive numbers suggest that some of those pieces are finally beginning to fall into place.

So go ahead. Take another sip of that coffee.

#2589. Three Stars: Miami vs Duke

The Miami Hurricanes beat the Duke Blue Devils today at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, FL, 36-25. Duke transfers Darian Mensah and Cooper Barkate had big games. The defense could not contain Blue Devils running back Nate Sheppard, but got off the field on a few third downs, plus forced a turnover. It wasn't the prettiest game, but I'll take it.

Quick rant: I know Miami won the game, but man, the refs were extra awful today. There were multiple missed pass interference calls, the softest personal foul I've seen against Elija Lofton, and a blatant missed holding call against Armondo Blount in the red zone where the next play went for a touchdown. Today is why Miami Hurricanes fans talk about officiating as often as we do. Ugh.

Let's get to the three stars of the game.

Miami's stud freshman running back played his best game of the season today. Mallory is officially one of the most talented and trusted offensive players on the 2026 Miami Hurricanes roster. He looks like a replicant of Frank Gore. The way Mallory ran through Duke's defense on the long catch-and-run touchdown as well as his fourth quarter 39-yard touchdown scamper. Oh, and Mallory picked up at least two linebacker blitzes head on, giving Mensah time to find a receiver. Coach Cristobal is lucky to have such a well-rounded running back behind Mark Fletcher Jr. Stats: 10 rushes, 71 yards, two touchdowns, three receptions, 79 yards, one touchdown.

The former Duke signal caller kept making plays today, despite his offensive line doing its best to provide as little protection as possible. Mensah was forced to scramble a ton. Luckily, his skill players did their part on catching the ball and making plays in the open field. Mensah only had the one touchdown pass to Mallory, but he made plenty of other quality throws. The play below was his highlight of the day in my opinion. Stat line: 30-41, 382 yards, one touchdown, zero turnovers, four rushes for seven yards. Love this dude.

The other high-profile Duke transfer had his second big game in a row post Malachi Toney's injury. Barkate showed it all today: route running, hands, speed, strength, wiggle. He really does have it all as a receiver. He's also faster than he looks. That 40-yard catch-and-run in the second quarter was impressive. It would be great to see Barkate finish with two more hundred-yard-plus games to close out the regular season. I love the way he is playing right now. Stats: 8 receptions for 134 yards.

Xavier Lucas – He's lucky that long touchdown pass on him in the fourth quarter didn't count. (Sigh). Besides that, Lucas had a huge interception early in the fourth quarter that helped seal the win.

Mohamed Toure – Toure led the Canes in tackles today with 11 total, 10 solo. I know Sheppard abused Miami defenders today, but I liked the way Toure tackled in space overall, especially compared to other Canes defenders.

Speaking of overall, Miami's defense is overall frustrating as hell. I am sure Cam will take them to task in G/B/U, but damn. And where is Damon Wilson? I don't see his name at all in the box score. Yikes.

Who were your three stars of the game? Let us know in the comments below.

#2587. Rockets fourth-quarter three-point shooting has been clutch

After their first two-game losing streak of the season, where the Houston Rockets suffered losses to the Dallas Mavericks and Phoenix Suns, the Rockets have quickly righted the ship, and after a suprisingly hard fought win over the Utah Jazz, the Rockets have now won three straight and are 10-3 on the season.

Alperen Sengun finished with the second-most points in a game in his career, carrying the Rockets with 43 points. The Rockets relinquished a 12-point lead early in the third quarter as the 1-11 Jazz actually took the lead at one point. The Rockets and Jazz traded blows for most of the third quarter, leading into the fourth.

In the fourth quarter, Sengun continued his dominance, controlling the game. Of course, his play had a lot to do with the Rockets' win, but another area that the Rockets have excelled at all season also played a big part. The Rockets entered the game as the league leaders in fourth-quarter three-point shooting.

The Rockets have been one of the best three-point shooting teams all season, coming into Friday's game ranked seventh overall from downtown at 37.4 percent. Some games are over early when one team dominates the other, and the result is never in doubt, but a lot of games come down to the last few minutes and become back-and-forth contests.

That is why the Rockets' league-leading fourth-quarter three-point shooting is so important. Several times this season, the Rockets have made multiple shots from downtown in a row in the final period, which completely shifts the momentum in a close game.

The Rockets have seen their fourth-quarter three-point shooting improve over the last three seasons. In the 2024-25 season, the Rockets were bottom five in this category; last season, they improved to tenth, and this season, they are the best in the league.

That happened again in Friday's win, as Bogdan Bogdanović and Kevin Durant each hit a huge three-pointer, with the Jazz cutting the lead to one late in the fourth quarter. The Rockets' fourth-quarter shooting matters in close regular-season games, but especially in high-pressure playoff games, and could be the difference between another first-round exit and the Rockets' first deep playoff run since the 2017-18 season.

#2585. Badgers embarrassed by Maryland for second straight year

The Wisconsin Badgers suffered an embarrassing 24-21 loss to the Maryland Terrapins for the second year in a row, once again raising questions about Luke Fickell and the direction of the program after the 31-10 win over Rutgers last weekend.

Wisconsin entered the week on a strong note, as they had dominated Rutgers in true freshman quarterback Ryan Hopkins's first start last weekend. They came into the game as 8.5-point favorites and were still in the mix in the Big Ten race with a 6-3 record and 4-2 conference record.

However, just like last weekend, the Badgers suffered a surprising loss. A season ago, Wisconsin was embarrassed 27-10 on their own home field, which sparked a six-game losing streak. This season, it was a 24-21 loss to one of the worst teams in the Big Ten this season.

Wisconsin opened the game on a high note, forcing a quick three-and-out on the first set of plays, while responding with a five-play, 57-yard touchdown drive. The Badgers got great field position and took advantage with a 21-yard Jaylon Domingeaux catch, a pass interference call, and a 17-yard Darrion Dupree run, leading to a four-yard touchdown run on the next play.

The Badgers allowed one first down on their next set of plays, but quickly forced a punt again and seemed to be picking up where they left off a week ago. But on 4th & 1 at their own 39-yard line, they decided to go for it with a fullback dive, and Ryan Schwendeman fumbled. Clearly, the Badgers didn't feel like a quarterback sneak was an option, and there was the lane to convert, but the fumble gave Maryland great field position.

Credit goes to the defense, though, who got help from the Terrapins with two false starts to force a quick three-and-out and get the ball back on a punt, albeit at Wisconsin's own 1-yard line. The Badgers went to Bryan Jackson twice, getting nothing, before a short pass on fourth down forced them to punt deep in their own territory.

Once again, Maryland got great field position, even with a penalty at the end of the punt, starting at their own 47-yard line. But the defense was stellar again, as it had been throughout the first quarter, and Maryland opened the second quarter with a missed 51-yard field goal.

Finally, the offense got some rhythm. Abu Sama, who was nowhere to be found in the first quarter, ripped an 18-yard run on his first touch, and Darrion Dupree followed that up with eight and 11-yard runs later in the drive to set up two more first downs. The Badgers got themselves in the red zone, but what has killed them all season hurt them again: a negative play on first down. That ended up derailing the drive, and they were forced to settle for a field goal.

Midway through the second quarter, the defense had their worst drive of the game so far. Without a pass rush affecting the quarterback, Cardell Williams ripped off six straight completions before a quarterback keeper for one yard ended up in the end zone. Suddenly, a game where the Badgers defense had dominated through the first 20+ minutes was 10-7 with three minutes left in the half.

Wisconsin went nowhere on its next drive, as Sama got just two yards before an incompletion and a sack on second and third down. So, the Badgers quickly punted, and Maryland got a great opportunity to tie the game up before halftime.

Once again, it was a ton of Cardell Williams, both with his arms and his legs, as Maryland's backup quarterback moved the ball down the field in the two-minute drill. Starting at Wisconsin's 40-yard line, the Terrapins had four rushes and two passes, getting all the way down to the one-yard line. But Matt Jung and Mason Posa forced a huge fumble on a one-yard carry, recovering the ball before halftime and saving a touchdown. Unfortunately, Jung was carted off with a leg injury, needing a cast on his foot.

The Badgers started with the ball in the second half, but their offense remained lifeless with another three-and-out, starting with a negative play. It really felt at this point that Jeff Grimes had no faith in his quarterback. The Badgers went screen (for -1), run (for five), and screen (for -2) for a three-and-out.

The defense bounced back from two shaky drives with a quick three-and-out, but the Badgers coughed it up immediately. After a first down drop, Darrion Dupree took the second-down handoff and fumbled after no gain, with Maryland recovering and returning it to the Wisconsin 16-yard line.

Four runs later, the Terrapins were in the end zone with a surprise 14-13 lead. Now, there was still a ton of ball game left, but Wisconsin's offense looked shattered, and they needed a turnaround fast with injuries piling up on the defensive side.

And it didn't look good at first. The Badgers got no gain on first down, one yard on a second-down screen, and nothing on third down for a quick three-and-out. But Sean West was roughed on the punt, giving Wisconsin a free 15 yards. That, plus an unsportsmanlike conduct, took the Badgers from their own 31 to the Maryland 39.

From there, Wisconsin went with five straight dropbacks, completing just one for 15 yards, which set up an easier field goal for Gavin Lahm from 41 yards, cutting the lead to 14-13.

Maryland's next drive was instantly killed by a false start and a holding penalty on the first two plays, and they quickly punted, with the Badgers getting the ball at their own 43-yard line.

Well, Wisconsin finally started to get a rhythm and consistently move the ball, with Ryan Hopkins having a couple of nice scrambles and Jeff Grimes mixing in an end around. The Badgers quickly moved into the red zone after a 28-yard Hopkins run and, two plays later, punched it in from the one-yard line for a Darrion Dupree touchdown.

Despite how poorly their offense had played, the Badgers were back on top, and they went for two to make it 21-14 at the top of the fourth quarter.

Maryland's offense was able to move a bit on its next drive, thanks to a 13-yard run from DeJuan Williams on 4th & 1 and a 15-yard penalty on backup safety Matthew Traynor, but its own holding penalty killed a very promising drive, as they punted in plus territory once again.

With 8:43 left, the Badgers started with the ball on their own 10-yard line. This felt like the perfect time for them to kill clock and start to move the ball a bit offensively. They didn't get a single yard, punting in less than a minute, and Maryland was in position to tie things up with 7:45 left.

Well, penalties were the Terrapins' Achilles ' heel. As their run game started to get going and they advanced to the Wisconsin 35-yard line, another unsportsmanlike conduct penalty came. Maryland didn't recover and, once again, punted in plus territory.

With 4:29 left on their own 20-yard line, could this be the drive for the Badgers to seal the deal? Darrion Dupree got five on the first play, but was stuffed on 2nd & 5. Then Ryan Hopkins fumbled a third-down snap, sending the Badgers back and forcing their fifth three-and-out of the game. Sean West's punt went just 35 yards to midfield, which the Terrapins returned to the Wisconsin 39.

One play later, the score was tied, as Cardell Williams hit Preston Howard for a 39-yard catch-and-run touchdown. Wisconsin had a ton of opportunities to close the game, and they never capitalized. But the game wasn't over, as the Badgers had the ball with 2:11 left and all their timeouts.

Things started great as Darrion Dupree took a screen 15 yards to get the Badgers a 1st & 10 at their own 40 at the 2-minute warning. Well, disaster struck after that, as Ryan Hopkins didn't identify a free rusher and was crushed by the blitzer, fumbling and getting hurt in the process.

So Maryland had the ball on the Wisconsin 33-yard line, needing just a field goal to take the lead. They ran the ball six times, getting one first down before kicking a field goal on 4th & 1 at Wisconsin's 12, securing the 24-21 lead.

The Badgers had just 29 seconds left with no timeouts and Colton Joseph in the game off the bench. Joseph committed an illegal forward pass on his first play, essentially sealing the game for the Badgers, and Wisconsin would go on to suffer its fourth loss of the season.

This was an ugly one for the Badgers. The offense compiled just 201 total yards, going 2 of 12 on third downs, as Ryan Hopkins had a rough day, averaging 3.5 yards per pass. They also committed three turnovers, gifting Maryland some great field position.

Defensively, the Badgers played well enough to win. They stopped the run, and the Terrapins went 2 of 13 on third downs. But they allowed Cardell Williams to get too comfortable in the pocket, marking the third time this year they've done that to a backup quarterback (Iowa, UCLA).

This is an embarrassing loss for the Badgers and one that requires some deep thinking about the direction of the program, given how inconsistent this team has been over the past few weeks.

#2584. NHL Power Rankings: Flyers flounder to start new season as Rick Tocchet searches for answers

I hate to get so negative just one week into the season, but the Philadelphia Flyers have forced my hand. After a magical run to the second round of the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, the Flyers have fallen on their face through four games.

Philadelphia opened the season with a 7-0 loss to the rival Pittsburgh Penguins, and coach Rick Tocchet described his team's play as "disturbing." There was only one way for the season to go after that, right? Wrong.

The Flyers are off to an 0-2-2 start, and the underlying numbers aren't pretty. Per Natural Stat Trick, they have a five-on-five expected goals share of 26.0%, which ranks last in the NHL. Their 4.57 xGA/60 also ranks last. Their 1.94 xGF/60? You guessed it. Last.

Tocchet's bunch entered the season with a lot of well-earned optimism. Even with subpar play from Matvei Michkov last season, the Flyers managed to reach the Eastern Conference Semifinals. Rookie Porter Martone asserted himself as a budding star with six goals and nine assists in 19 games between the regular season and playoffs.

There's still plenty of time -- 80 games exactly -- for the Flyers to get back on track and restore that optimism, but to say this has been a discouraging start would be an understatement.

#2583. D’Angelo Russell and LaMelo Ball: Darling vs. Discarded

Just a few years ago, the Minnesota Timberwolves made a deal for an enigmatic, polarizing point guard using a first-round pick and a franchise legend (do not disrespect Andrew Wiggins, that's my guy), just as they did in this offseason. The Wolves were universally lambasted for this move, with their trade partner being praised for selling high.

D'Angelo Russell is one of the most reviled Wolves of recent history. Despite a few decent years (or months), his turnovers, early shot-clock off-the-dribble threes, and miserable defense led to a benching in the playoffs against the Memphis Grizzlies for Jordan McLaughlin, and his reputation with the fanbase never really recovered. Maybe it's partly that Russell was the outgoing piece on one of the best trades the Wolves franchise have ever pulled off that made him so infinitely laugh-at-able for fans.

Still, Russell's first few months in a Wolves jersey ahead of the COVID lockdown were like lightning in a bottle. Those same fans who now laugh at him were celebrating what he brought to the team in a season that began with Treveon Graham in the starting lineup.

That feels a lot like Wolves fans clamoring for LaMelo Ball as a second star who brings joy instead of moodiness and moroseness.

But the question then becomes a sad one of whether caution is necessary at a time that is so full of joy. Despite the absence of Anthony Edwards, the Timberwolves are on a five-game win streak on the shoulders of Ball. After multiple years of joyless, winning basketball, the Wolves have their heart back. So is that question even worth asking? Is this piece worth writing?

The obvious answer is no. The big difference in LaMelo Ball and D'Angelo Russell's first 12 games for the Wolves is that Minnesota has gone 9-3 with Ball at the helm, an equal reflection of Russell's 3-9.

And yes, the team around these players was far worse in the 2019-20 season than it is now, but still, Minnesota is winning with one young star point guard leading the charge, when his apparent predecessor couldn't do so.

To add to it, the view of the trade is so vastly different already this season. The Golden State Warriors traded Russell, Omari Spellman, and Jacob Evans III for Andrew Wiggins and a top-3 protected first-round pick, which eventually landed at seventh overall and became Jonathan Kuminga (hey, look at that!). Even within that lightning stretch from Russell, Wiggins was playing incredibly well next to Steph Curry. When the draft lottery arrived a few months later, the Wolves landed Anthony Edwards at first-overall, the Warriors took James Wiseman (which was always a bad choice), and the Charlotte Hornets took Ball.

The Warriors would go on to win a title with Wiggins taking his play to another level as the clear second option on offense and an absolutely rabid rebounder, while Russell was quickly downgraded to the third option for a team that was still bottom-10 in the NBA. That certainly played a part.

But now, Naz Reid is miserable in Charlotte, the first rounder the Wolves sent the Hornets is seven years out and completely out of mind, and Ball is playing his way into an All-Star – dare I say an All-NBA – nod.

The perception is entirely opposite, which means that any step back will hurt so much more. Wolves fans have bought in, they've signed up, they've gone to war for this player and this team in a way they hadn't, because the night-to-night performances are consistent and fun. I mean, honestly, we went so hard at an online NBA analyst that he went on a Wolves podcast, got succinctly disproven, and was successfully converted into a believer.

So why can't I shake the feeling of deja vu, that feeling that maybe the Wolves' new star point guard has what it takes to take the Wolves out of the plateau they've been at, one that was eventually only half paid off with Russell.

Ball has been more than a dream outcome so far this season. Reid, as beloved as he was, was always a low price to pay for the guy who was bringing Moussa Diabate into Amare Stoudemire conversations in the context of the Hornets playing to the statistical level of the Run-and-Gun Phoenix Suns. Minnesota got a 6'7 orchestrator and offensive maestro for pennies on the dollar, which is not what they gave up for Russell.

I guess the answer is the same one that I came to in 2020, when Minnesota finished with one of the worst records in the league. While stuck in lockdown, longing for some Wolves basketball, I would hang around and watch the same "Track the Pack" episode welcoming Russell to Minnesota, followed by highlight after highlight of the Malik Beasley, D'Angelo Russell, and Jarred Vanderbilt Wolves.

I chose to enjoy it then. I choose to enjoy this now.

Hopefully, this version of Ball is more real than those first 12 games of Russell were. Hopefully, Minnesota keeps winning behind their point guard of the future. Hopefully, Anthony Edwards returns to an offensive ecosystem that has survived without him, but reaches a new level with him.

But, in the meantime, let's enjoy the team that exists, and remember that comparisons and contrasts do not always come from a place of sad disrespect. Let's enjoy this, Wolves fans. Fun doesn't always last, but it's certainly better now than it has been in years.

Maybe, just maybe, the most fun since that 12-game stretch where Minnesota and fans were sure they had found their joy in D'Angelo Russell.

#2581. NFL predictions: In Browns-Texans, Cleveland needs to turn the corner to become a serious threat

This Sunday, the Cleveland Browns (5-4) take on the Houston Texans (3-5). Below, we analyze a few advantages, disadvantages, or general thoughts about the two teams before getting to our predictions for the game.

The start to the season for the Cleveland Browns was a feel-good story. Todd Monken in his first year as a head coach, all of the young players shining at times, and Deshaun Watson having five game-winning drives. And it was fun to harp on the incredible stat of all of those victories having game-winning drives, but we all know that isn't sustainable. If the Browns want to contend for the postseason the rest of the year, something has to change.

Playing every winnable game down-to-the-wire hasn't gone away.

The run game issues on both sides haven't gone away.

I praised Todd Monken and Mike Rutenberg earlier this season for their ability to adapt and make adjustments. I don't think that has stalled, I think what we're seeing now are the true weaknesses of this team, and they aren't marks of a playoff contender. Cleveland's hopes seem to rest on taking advantage of their easy schedule, but they've blown their margin for error in that category too with losses to the Jets and Saints.

I think the coaching staff is trying to get it fixed each week, but so far they've mostly come up empty. That doesn't mean the team can't turn the corner in some of those areas, but the thing I keep saying now is, "this is the team's four-game home stretch." I don't necessarily expect them to win all four games, which would put them at a ridiculous 7-0 at home, but on a game-by-game basis, we need to see this team pull of a dominant performance somewhere. Something to further bolster their confidence, further establish their identity, and to ride for the rest of the season.

As a follow-up to the above, there is one X-factor who could, at any point, make a monumental difference to the team. Let's get into it with some of our miscellaneous notes this week:

That X-factor would be……….DE Jared Verse. It's been a storyline all season — he was brought here, not to replicate what Myles Garrett did, but to be a damn-good alternative to him, at least when it comes to pressuring the quarterback. Overall, despite the run defense woes, the Browns' defense has been fairly solid this season, and the sacks are coming from everywhere but the edge. If Cleveland's defense is doing this good with Verse being a non-factor, or dare I say it, a liability, what is the upside to this unit if the switch finally flips for him?

We've hated on Verse a lot, but this week, he finally admitted that he hasn't played to the standard he wants, and that he's talked to the team's psychiatrist about it. I'm a firm believer in how the mental aspects of things can screw with your game. We see it most obviously with kickers all the time. Sometimes we see it with receivers and their drops. I thought Deshaun Watson had a mental block the past several years that he finally seems to have cleared. It's possible it's there with Verse. Verse says it's not physical, so something has to explain the extreme dropoff of being one of the league's best to one of the league's worst performing players. Maybe this is a step to somewhat tackling whatever is getting in the way of him being the player he's proven he can be. If he can deliver that against the Texans, maybe it's the boost that Cleveland needs to put away a game.

That presents us with the unique challenge of trying to figure out which Houston Texans team we'll see. C.J. Stroud has been a bit of a disappointment the past few years, and last year, the team went on an incredible stretch to close out the year due to their defense. This season, I feel like the defense has been crap, and Stroud is lighting it up most weeks. But this defense should be better; they've often been plagued by giving up big plays in pass defense.

Cleveland's pass defense needs to be up to the challenge this week. Although some teams have used the run lately to combat the Browns, I feel like Houston won't be so committed to the ground game.

Deshaun Watson starting over Shedeur Sanders this week is probably the right call. As much as I enjoyed Sanders finally letting loose in the fourth quarter and overtime last week, many of those plays aren't sustainable. When it was time to read-and-react in the first several quarters, things were too slow still, the operation was off, etc. The offense has had similar slow starts with Watson, of course, but the operation for the most part has been smooth with him.

According to FanDuel, the Browns are 4.5 point underdogs against the Texans. The over/under is 40.5.

Offensive coordinator Travis Switzer talked about how the team has tried to work on ways to start faster offensively:

"Yeah, the first thing as a staff, we looked at everything that we've done early in games, and when we looked at it, it was like, man, we've kind of tried a little bit of everything as far as, hey, let's maybe call some can plays early, or we've tried running it early. We've tried movement passes. So, we looked at that, and nothing really spiked out as far as, hey, this is the direction we should go there. And then we've also just stressed it to the guys, especially early in practice, like Wednesdays, the first period is always a tempo period, the first team period, so we've tried to stress it there. It's like, okay, we're going fast, but also, hey, we're trying to start fast. That's the point of this period here. And yeah, I can't say that it's been like one thing that jumped out to us. We just got to keep attacking it and try to stress it and just try to get better there."

Defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg was asked about Jared Verse's admission that he's seen the team psychiatrist to try to be a better pass rusher:

"I'm not going to discuss Jared Verse in terms of what he does off the field, but I'm really proud of Jared for his approach, for his attitude, the way he's working with his teammates and our D-line coaching staff to help himself get to where he wants to go."

Special teams coordinator Bryon Storer was asked about gunners when they run out of bounds (as Cleveland did last week):

"All right, so when you're putting the ball, you're putting it toward – usually you're trying to punt it toward the boundary to shorten the field. And so, you have releases by the gunners toward the punt direction. So, you'd like for both your gunners to release the same direction. So, if you're punting left, both guys release left, and one guy ends up into the boundary. Now, you can't run out of bounds on your own. A lot of times those corners will force you into the white. And so now you have to, take a line to re-enter. You know, what happened on that play was, DT (Daniel Thomas) didn't realize he had gotten in the white, and so we just had a discussion on the sideline and just said, 'hey, if there's any possibility that you could have gone out of bounds, all you got to do is just point to the ball, tell your teammates, you, you, you, and they touch it.' So, it's a big learning experience for us, and unfortunately, it cost us 30 yards of field position, so we had to learn the hard way. But I just don't think that it's possible to change what we do in terms of staying out of bounds. That's just part of the deal."

Here are predictions from multiple staff members at DBN:

Chris Pokorny: "The Browns have played a lot of close games, and are 3-0 at home, so this four-game home stretch that they are beginning is vital for them to stay in the playoff race. The Browns' pass defense has remained a strong suit, but offensively, they still have some consistency issues, with too many dry stretches of scoring. Of all the games the Browns have played this season, this is the one where I feel like I have no idea what to expect. C.J. Stroud seems to be playing at an unexpectedly high level, but the Browns' pass defense has been solid. Will Houston commit to the run, which Cleveland hasn't been able to stop for weeks? And while Houston's defense has struggled compared to my expectations, the talent seems to still be there, so do they get back on track against their former quarterback who takes a lot of sacks?" Browns 24, Texans 21

Jared Mueller: "The Browns are 3-0 at home, are coming off two straight losses, and Deshaun Watson takes back over at quarterback after a one-week concussion-related hiatus. The Texans have not been that good this year but have regrouped a bit and could have a healthy defense on the road in Cleveland.

For some reason, Jared Verse's admission of flaws is a confidence builder for me, despite Houston's talented offense." Browns 27, Texans 24

Thomas Moore: "I don't even know what to make of this team anymore. They win when it seems like all hope is lost, but then lose to the likes of the Jets and the Saints. The Texans will present a challenge, especially with their pass rush, but it's hard to know how good they are, either, because two of their three wins have come against the Titans and Chargers. The thought of the Browns going into the bye week on a three-game losing streak and having everyone bleat for the next two weeks about a quarterback change is too much to even consider." Browns 17, Texans 14

Barry Shuck: "Before the season began, I believed that the Texans would be one of the four best teams in the AFC. I also choose the wrong women. And although Houston might not make the playoffs, they have won three of their last four games and scored 44 points last weekend. The Texans have a prolific passing attack and the Browns are ranked #13 against the pass, so that will be a good chess match. They can't run the ball, but neither can the Browns. Cleveland is middle of the pack in their passing game while Houston is listed in the lower third defending the pass. So, maybe the Browns can air it out to Harold Fannin and either of their two rookie receivers. Defense, or lack of, will be the determining factor. Cleveland will need to find ways to finish drives. Thank goodness for a good kicker and punter." Texans 27, Browns 20

Ezweav: "We're definitely hitting the rough patch. It's a little promising watching the A22 against the Saints and seeing so many wide open plays (mostly missed) but the Texans aren't the Saints so it'll probably be a tougher slog

Defense should hold their own but CJ Stroud is a real quarterback so I don't love the matchup.  We'll probably be talking about how 5-5 still exceeds preseason expectations tomorrow afternoon." Texans 23, Browns 19

Curtiss Brown: "This game will be about as close of a playoff type game as can be. Considering what's at stake, it should be. The Houston Texans have been one of the bigger disappointments this season. As talented as the Texans defense is, they haven't been nearly as dominant. The Texans defense isn't really special in terms of scheme but the talent is there. The run defense is somewhat leaky and they are suspect to give up explosive plays in the passing game.

Houston's offense is starting to click a bit. Quarterback CJ Stroud might force the Texans to back up the Brinks truck if he finds a way to keep up this play. Houston will be down a couple of key defensive players so the Browns must take advantage of it.

Depending on how Houston comes out this game could be close or it turns into a route. If Houston comes out flat and underestimates the Browns, this could be a close game for 4 quarters. Houston might be down a couple players and are prone to letdowns but I feel that their talent will overcome that against a Browns team that is continuing to find themselves. Wouldn't surprise me if Cleveland stunned Houston but I dont see that happening." Texans 30, Browns 24 (OT)

#2580. Sabalenka sorry for outburst in Svitolina defeat

Aryna Sabalenka apologized on Saturday after an on-court outburst during her defeat to Ukrainian rival Elina Svitolina at the WTA Finals in Indian Wells.

Footage shared widely on social media appeared to show the former world number one swearing in a tirade that some commenters interpreted as directed towards Svitolina or Ukrainians in general.

However, Sabalenka said Saturday that she lost her cool due to the behavior of spectators during Friday's 3-6, 6-3, 1-6 defeat, which sent the four-time Grand Slam-winner crashing out.

"I want to clarify something from my recent match that has been circulating online," Sabalenka wrote in a post on Instagram.

"My comment was not directed at Elina. I was frustrated with a small group of spectators who were aggressively cheering my mistakes and I reacted emotionally in the moment.

"That said, I should have handled my frustration differently and I apologise to anyone I offended. Elina played a great match, and I wish her all the best for the rest of the tournament."

Svitolina has refused to shake hands with tennis players from Russia and its regional ally Belarus since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

#2579. Game Preview: Nets close out the road trip in Memphis

The Brooklyn Nets saw what "worse" looked like on Wednesday night against the New Orleans Pelicans. Brooklyn certainly has its issues, but they pale in comparison to the nightmare New Orleans fans have to sit through right now. The Nets cruised to a 145-111 blowout victory. Yeesh.

Tonight's opponent, however, has been one of the pleasant surprises of the 2026-27 NBA season. The Memphis Grizzlies enter Saturday at 8-4 and in great shape — though, much like Brooklyn, they just beat the stuffing out of those same Pelicans, rolling to a 142-111 win last night. My goodness.

Matchup: Brooklyn Nets (3-8) at Memphis Grizzlies (8-4)

Probable – Nolan Traore (right calf soreness/tightness)

OUT – Joshua Jefferson (G League Assignment)

OUT – Tyler Bilodeau (G League – Two-Way)

OUT – Zach Edey (left ankle injury management)

OUT – Scotty Pippen Jr (lumbar disc herniation)

OUT – Richie Saunders (right knee surgery)

This is night two of a back-to-back for the Grizzlies. However, nobody played over 30 minutes last night so theoretically everyone should be good to go. We'll see.

Grizzlies head coach Tuomas Iisalo has this offense humming this season, and this breakdown by Adam Pike dives into some of his favorite actions. He's earned complete buy-in from this young roster, and the early results have been promising so far.

Memphis' most promising cornerstone is someone the franchise hopes carries them into the next generation. Rookie Cameron Boozer adjusted to the NBA seamlessly and somehow still has plenty of room to grow. He's second among rookies in assists per game, a pretty impressive feat for a power forward, alongside 9.8 rebounds a night. And watching Boozer also makes me realize I watched his dad's journey from college at Duke all the way to the pros and beyond. Time flies, man.

Boozer will draw plenty of Julius Randle. After Wednesday's win, Randle praised the organization and structure of Brooklyn's offense. It also helped that they only committed 15 turnovers as a team, their second lowest amount this season. When you actually get shots up at the rim, good things tend to happen.

Brooklyn will need a big night out of Day'ron Sharpe to steal a road win. Memphis is third in the NBA in rebounding (47.9 RPG) this season, and Sharpe is still Brooklyn's best weapon on the glass. Sharpe has been steady this year and the Nets are going to need him to hold Boozer, Isaiah Stewart, and the rest of the Grizzlies' frontcourt off the offensive boards.

There are two schools of thought related to Egor Demin. One is to praise for maintaining good three-point percentages while taking a high volume of threes when he's on the court. That success can carry him a long way and guarantee he's always on the court. The other is to express worry that he hasn't been getting to the rim at rates that make the defense worry about him inside the arc.

As of this writing, he's averaging six drives to the rim per game and his frequency of shots at the rim is greater than what it was last year. However, it's only seven shots at the rim so you can't read that much into it.

Demin is going to have to add more to his game if he wants to reach that next level. And we'll see if tonight's the night Demin and Mikel Brown Jr get real minutes on the court tonight.

MBJ is listed as questionable, so we'll see if he's back out there. It's been a frustrating experience for a lot of Nets fans, and it's understandable. This team has to figure out what their future is and fast, and that comes with getting your youngsters real minutes together so you can properly evaluate what's working and what's not.

It's always fun watching a player's steady ascent pay off. Ty Jerome has been an analytics-crowd favorite for the past couple of seasons, and this year he's putting it all together. He's averaging a career high 25.4 points and 5.3 assists per game and is outpacing other franchise cornerstones such as Cade Cunningham and Nikola Jokic.

Even as the Griz kids gain more experience, Jerome will be essential to their growth remains the engine making it work. From Maxwell Ogden at Beale Street Bears:

"As a proven sharpshooter and shot creator, Jerome can play with just about any combination of his teammates. He's just as lethal when working off of scorers and playmakers as he is when he creates his own shots. Furthermore, his mere presence on the court means defenses have to relax the attention they give to the less experienced Grizzlies players."

I'm a sucker for rewarding career role players with All-Star appearances when they're having career years, so I'm hoping Jerome gets the nod this winter.

#2577. Why Ziaire Williams credits ‘crazy’ Dillon Brooks for NBA success

Why Ziaire Williams credits 'crazy' Dillon Brooks for NBA success appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

LOS ANGELES –  The Los Angeles Lakers wrap up a four-game road trip on Sunday with a matchup against the Phoenix Suns. Opposite the Lakers will be Suns wing Dillon Brooks, one of the NBA's most tenacious and intense players, and a long-time thorn in their side. But for new Lakers forward Ziaire Williams, who has made a major impact for the team this season, much of what he does on the court can be attributed to his former teammate.

Prior to joining the Lakers, Ziaire Williams spent the first three seasons of his career with the Memphis Grizzlies, the first two playing alongside Dillon Brooks. Brooks joined the Houston Rockets via sign and trade in the 2023 offseason, but not before imparting his wisdom on Williams and setting the foundation for him to have a successful NBA career.

"Dillon, he is one of my favorite teammates ever. As crazy as he is, the complete opposite off the court. It's amazing how he's able to flip that switch. He was like the ultimate vet, he always looked out for me, always. Just made sure I was good, gave me tips, especially on the defensive end," Williams said after Lakers' practice on Friday. "I credit a lot of the knowledge and the success I've had from Dillon."

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Williams came into the league as a lottery pick, No. 10 overall in the 2021 NBA Draft. He was thrust into a regular role from the get-go playing in 62 games as a rookie, including 31 starts, at a little over 21 minutes per game. The Grizzlies were a 50-win team at the time as well, looking to contend in the Western Conference.

For a young player like Williams, being able to ease the transition and meet the expectations of a winning team had a lot to do with Brooks. He's very much looking forward to seeing his old teammate again when the Lakers face off against the Suns, as Brooks taught him, there's no pleasantries to be exchanged as opponents.

"Being a young player, he almost instilled that foundation for me, along with Taylor Jenkins who was our coach at the time. Both of them, they were big role models for me," Williams said. "I love Dillon. Great player, great competitor, no friends on the court though. I'm sure we'll be going at it."

As far as Williams' season with the Lakers, he's putting up career numbers across the boards. He's averaging a career-best 11.0 points, 2.6 rebounds, 2.0 assists and 1.5 steals while shooting 56.3 percent from the field, 46.5 percent from the 3-point line and 83.3 percent from the free-throw line. His assists, steals and shooting percentages from the field and 3-point range are all career-highs.

He's also alternated between starting and coming off the bench while playing a little over 24 minutes per game. With the Lakers on the tail end of the road trip, Williams reflected on how he's continued to bond with his teammates and build chemistry amid being tied with the San Antonio Spurs for the best record in the NBA at 11-2.

"I think I grew a lot, not even just on the court, but just being around my teammates more. More flights, more bus rides, so small things that help you build chemistry. It doesn't always happen on the court," Williams said. "I love these guys. It's fun to come into work every day, it's fun to travel with them, it's never a dull moment. It's just a great group of guys … definitely built some chemistry for sure."

#2574. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2573. Colorado State basketball unsettled in upset loss to Loyola-Chicago

A no good, very bad half of basketball cost Colorado State.

The Ram men's basketball team often looked listless and disjointed as visiting Loyola-Chicago manhandled the Rams on both ends of the floor in the first half on Nov. 14 at Moby Arena.

It ended in an 73-58 loss for CSU, in a game analytical projections had the Rams as likely winners by 10-12 points.

By the intermission the Rams (3-1) were down 20 points (44-24) and Loyola-Chicago (3-1) had as many field goals made (17) as CSU had attempted.

Loyola-Chicago's athletic, aggressive defense clearly disrupted CSU and the Rams couldn't get into their offense.

The Rams turned the ball over 11 times in the first half alone. And when they did get a shot, it didn't go well as CSU was just 4-17 (24%) shooting in the first half.

And the defensive end wasn't any better. Loyola-Chicago was over 50% in the first half on both 3-pointers and field goals. And when the Ramblers missed? CSU was bullied on the glass and in the paint.

Loyola-Chicago's lead grew to 23 in the first minute of the second half. The Rams did claw back some with a better second-half effort. The defense improved and the offense found some footing, mostly led by freshman guard Pops Dunson.

Still, the closest CSU came was within nine points at 67-58 with 2:49 to go. But even then, CSU showed its vulnerabilities.

The Rams had three-straight possessions with turnovers shortly after Booth's 3-pointer and that ended any hopes of a wild comeback.

Booth finished with 12 points and 13 rebounds. Dunson scored 13 points.

But the overall numbers are ugly for CSU. The Rams had 18 turnovers and Loyola-Chicago outrebounded CSU 40-31. The Ramblers had eight offensive rebounds and outscored CSU 28-10 in the paint.

Loyola-Chicago lost 107-93 at Air Force earlier in the week.

This isn't a catastrophic loss for CSU's season, but it's a significant early negative mark on the resume. More importantly, it's a significant early-season test to see if or how CSU grows and responds from this.

Next up is a Nov. 18 home game against North Dakota State.

#2569. Kings head coach Doug Christie gets brutally honest about job security

SACRAMENTO ― The Sacramento Kings have dropped another game and if you think head coach Doug Christie is worried about being in some kind of hot seat, he's not. And he shouldn't be.

It's a familiar position for Christie, who's been dealt a bad hand since his head coaching tenure began. He inherited a then-Mike Brown team that was a season removed from the postseason before eventually trading its franchise player, De'Aaron Fox. They finished 40-42, Christie went 27-24 as interim, having taken over after a 13-18 start.

Last season, as an official first-year coach, without the interim tag, multiple players in his projected lineup, including Domantas Sabonis and Keegan Murray, missed large portions of the season, and the Kings finished with its worst record in franchise history since moving to Sacramento at 22-60.

And now, the Kings are having one of the worst starts in franchise history, dropping to 1-11 after their Friday night loss to the Portland Trail Blazers, 120-107, on Nov. 13 during the NBA Cup. It's the worst start since the 1990-91 season, in which that team started 1-13.

"I think this seat is hot always, so it doesn't really matter," Christie told USA TODAY about potentially being in the hot seat. "Obviously, we want to win games. Nobody wants to win more than me, from the standpoint that the record doesn't go on the player's numbers. The record goes on coach's number."

When Scott Perry became Kings general manager in April 2025, one of his first moves was to sign Christie to a three-year deal, worth about $2 million per year with a team option in the final year, 2027-28. Christie remained leading the charge after coaching to the worst franchise record in team history since 2008-2009 (17-65), as Perry attributed that tumultuous season to injuries, according to The Athletic.

It's much of the same this season, with a season-ending injury to Ben Simmons and second-year center Maxime Raynaud missing the start of the season with a knee injury.

"We come in, continue to teach, continue to push," Christie said. "As we get all these guys back and get them healthy, and then we continue down the path of trying to put together what we thought we would be putting together when we started this process."

The Kings are reportedly hesitant to part ways with Christie, according to The Athletic's Sam Amick. Former Sacramento Kings legend and current Sacramento State head coach Mike Bibby sat front row to get a witness of the the beatdown handed to the Kings.

The former guard, who played in Sacramento from 2001-2008, showed support for his former teammate, saying he wasn't the one to blame during a postgame appearance with Morgan Ragan and Deuce Mason on NBC Sports California.

"I don't blame Doug (Christie)," Bibby said. "I don't think Doug is the problem. Doug's been there for a long time, I think Doug could help, but getting rid of Doug's not the problem."

However, Bibby did say it was "time for some changes". Although he wasn't sure where those changes needed to come from, he advised the team to trade guys like Domantas Sabonis, Zach LaVine and Malik Monk to put them in better positions while the Kings start over. It happened to Bibby in his day when the Kings were no longer winning and they traded him to the Atlanta Hawks in 2008.

"When I was here I didn't wanna leave, but it was time to go," Bibby said. "For those guys put them in good situations like Sabonis, LaVine, put them in situations that could help them and get some good stuff back. It's going to take a couple of years to get the Kings going again."

Kings: Darius Acuff Jr. is making history, but is losing taking a toll?

If there's one thing Christie knows, it's how hard the Sacramento fans go for the Kings. He's experienced it as a player, and as both assistant and head coach he's seen how they've stuck beside the team through multiple years of losing seasons and the breakthrough when they finally cracked the postseason after a 16-year drought.

Christie's message to the fans: "it won't always be like this."

"This is a process that we're going through to try to get to where we want to go, and their loyalty means everything," Christie told USA TODAY. " When I see them around town, they're always (saying) 'coach keep going, keep pushing,' and that's what I do every day. I'll always be the first one in the building, working until we figure this thing out."

Kings forward Keegan Murray had a similar message to the fans to keep supporting, despite the shortcomings.

"I love our fans. They've been great to us... to me. I appreciate them coming out to support, we know that Rome's not built in a day but at the end of the day we're trying," Murray told USA TODAY. "With their support, it'll only get better."

Murray, Sabonis and Monk are the few Kings players that have been around for their lone playoff appearance in the last 15 years. Murray often tells the team, especially Acuff who was down in the dumps after a recent home loss, about how loud Golden 1 Center can get when their team is rolling.

"When we're really good, this place is better than any arena in the NBA," Murray said. "I feel like that's a big motivating factor in what we're trying to get to. ... I'm just hoping we can get back on track."

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Kings head coach Doug Christie gets brutally honest about job security

#2567. Austria seal top spot with win over Republic of Ireland

Republic of Ireland's hopes of securing top spot and automatic promotion to League A were ended by Austria after they suffered a 1-0 defeat in their penultimate Nations League Group B3 game at the Raiffeisen Arena.

Substitute Sasa Kalajdzic poked home from a corner to score the winner on 79 minutes as Austria preserved their unbeaten home record, which stretches back to October 2023.

The defeat in Linz, Republic of Ireland's second away loss in the group, leaves Heimir Hallgrimsson's side third, a point behind Kosovo, who they face in their final game on Tuesday.

A win in that fixture in Dublin would ensure a second-place finish and Republic of Ireland's place in pot two for the Euro 2028 qualifying draw in December.

Austria, who fought back from two goals down to take a point against the Irish in Dublin last month, started well and tested Caoimhin Kelleher just two minutes in as he was forced to get down low to turn Christoph Baumgartner's deflected strike behind.

The Irish grew into the game and threatened for the first time on 22 minutes as Troy Parrott connected with Dara O'Shea's delivery from the left, but his acrobatic effort was dealt with by Alexander Schlager.

The Real Betis striker went close again soon after when his rising strike from range was tipped over by the goalkeeper.

At the other end, Kelleher produced a fine reflex save to push Christoph Lang's half-volley over the crossbar before Michael Gregoritsch, who scored in the 2-2 draw in Dublin, then blasted over.

Austria continued to push for the opener in the second half as Gregoritsch's glancing header from a corner landed on the roof of the net and Kelleher then made two good saves to thwart Kevin Danso and Baumgartner.

The RB Leipzig midfielder looked certain to break the deadlock after the hour mark when he raced into the box, but skewed a shot horribly wide.

Momentum shifted back to Republic of Ireland in this end-to-end encounter as Ryan Manning and Parrott both drew flying saves from Schlager.

Gregoritsch's fizzing strike from a short free-kick routine was saved by Kelleher, before the hosts did make a spell of sustained pressure count 11 minutes from time.

Gregoritsch met a deep corner and headed the ball back across goal, with Kelleher only able to push the ball into the path of Kalajdzic, who stabbed home on the line.

Substitute Chiedozie Ogbene squandered a golden chance to equalise on 86 minutes as he headed straight at Schlager after connecting with Liam Scales' super ball in as the Irish left Linz empty handed.

Republic of Ireland have won just one of their five Nations League games [Getty Images]

Hallgrimsson spoke in the build-up to the game that he wanted his side to cut out mistakes and be braver in Linz.

He emphasised that second point by selecting an attack-minded line-up.

Finn Azaz dropped into a deeper roll to accommodate Adam Idah and Jack Moylan behind Parrott after the three linked so well in the 3-0 win over Israel, as the Irish chased a victory which would keep their hopes of winning the group alive.

After a shaky opening, Hallgrimsson's side settled and produced a spirited display, but they ultimately lacked the clinical edge to finish any of the numerous opportunities they created.

Their talisman Parrott, who had 10 goals in his last seven competitive games but is without a goal in eight for his club, failed to beat Schlager with his three clear-cut chances while Idah and Moylan cut peripheral figures in a frustrating evening in front of goal.

The ever-reliable Kelleher kept the Irish in the game at times with some big saves in an entertaining game, but he was powerless to stop Kalajdzic's winning goal.

Hallgrimsson will be frustrated his side failed to deal with the corner before it fell to Kalajdzic to score, which was ultimately the defining moment in a tight game.

They pressed hard for a late leveller, with Austria hanging on at times, but defeat ends their hopes of topping the group.

Republic of Ireland will take confidence from how well they competed with Austria across the two games, but to come away with just a point having played well home and away, will be tough to take.

Their hopes of trying to win promotion to League A for the first time are not all lost, but they now must produce against Kosovo, who they suffered defeat against last month, to secure second place and a promotion play-off, which would have been the aim heading into this campaign.

Jalen Sundell was notably not fined for his unnecessary roughness penalty on Zach Charbonnet's big catch-and-run, which feels like an unofficial way to say that there should've been no flag on the play.
